header.name: Random walk and Brownian motion
header.description: A question related to random walk (RW) was asked  by Karl Pearson in a letter to Nature (1905), which Lord Rayleigh answered in the next issue where he hinted a solution via Brownian motion (BM). Einstein in 1905 described the movement of pollen in the atmosphere via a heat equation whose solution (obtained much later) suggested Brownian motion (name after Robert Brown who did empirical investigations on the movement of pollen in water). Polya (1910) gave a rigorous mathematical structure of RW and carried out the first significant mathematical work on the topic. Later over the last century researchers worked on the topic and now it is ubiquitous in the study of stochastic processes. Donsker’s theorem states that the diffusive limit of a RW (i.e. suitably scaled in time and space) converges in distribution to the BM. In the last two decades BM attained importance in mathematical finance through the Black-Scholes equation relating to the movement of stock prices
prerequisites_mandatory: MTH 371: Stochastic Processes and Applications, or equivalent.

outcomes.label: CO1
outcomes.raw_text: Markov chains are ubiquitous in modeling real-life phenomenon. This course starts with the fundamentals of random walk.

outcomes.label: CO2
outcomes.raw_text: Learn about recurrence and transition of random walks and other properties of random walks.

outcomes.label: CO3
outcomes.raw_text: Learn about Brownian motion which is fundamental in studying financial mathematics

outcomes.label: CO4
outcomes.raw_text: Learn how diffusive scaling of random walk yields a Brownian motion (Donsker’s theorem).
